intro: You play a young woman who uses a wheelchair and wants to be an architect in a small German town. Steps, cobblestones and forms stand in her way, and her eye for space and design is a real skill. Playing her means seeing how much of the world is built for one kind of body.

stairs.why: No lift, no ramp: a staircase is a wall. She cannot take this shortcut and must find another way.

rope.why: Cobbles and uneven ground jolt a wheelchair. Every metre costs more effort and time.

ramp.why: Lena knows every step-free route in town and uses it without a detour.

quiet.why: Drawing and designing are where she shines. Her best ideas come when she can focus on a plan.

advantage.title: Plan B ready
advantage.text: Lena's team and her habit of planning an alternative entrance move her forward. After rolling, add 2 to your result.

life.title: A small town (fictional)
life.text: Lena is an invented character. She is 12, uses a wheelchair after a spinal injury as a child, and loves drawing houses and bridges. The old market square is cobbled, and many shops have steps.

life.title: Which school?
life.text: The nearest school has no lift. The special school is an hour away by bus. Her parents fight for months to get a place at the local school with a ramp and support.

life.title: Friends and Ms Berger
life.text: At her new school classmates quickly stop noticing the chair. Her teacher, Ms Berger, makes sure class trips go to places Lena can reach.

life.title: Left out of the trip
life.text: In year 9 the trip goes to a hostel with no lift. Lena is told she can "stay home or be carried". Her friends refuse to go until the plans change.

life.title: Who else uses a ramp?
life.text: Lena notices that step-free access helps more people than just wheelchair users.

q.q: Which group also benefits from a step-free entrance?
a: Parents with prams and people with heavy luggage
q.x: Step-free design helps parents, older people, cyclists and delivery staff. Many accessible features are useful for everyone.

life.title: Forms for university
life.text: Lena applies to study architecture. Some lecture halls and studios are not accessible. Support and technical aids mean many forms and months of waiting.

life.title: A flat of her own
life.text: After 40 viewings, many landlords saying "it isn't suitable" before she even visits, Lena finds a small accessible flat near the university.

life.title: The professor's question
life.text: A professor asks whether she can do site visits. She answers with a plan: site photos, drones, a partner on site.

q.q: What is the main problem on an inaccessible building site?
q.x: The barrier is the missing access, not the person. Flexible solutions and adapted workplaces help everyone.

life.title: Her degree
life.text: Lena graduates with a design for an accessible community centre. Her professor calls it the best of the year.

life.title: Interviews
life.text: At job interviews Lena is asked about her "limitations" and the cost of adapting the office. Several offices have no step-free entrance.

life.title: An inclusive firm
life.text: A mid-sized firm hires Lena and adapts her workspace within two weeks. Wider doors and lower lift buttons help the whole team.

life.title: Designing for everyone
life.text: Lena helps plan a market square with level paths, then opens her own studio for accessible design. She says: "I'm not stuck in a wheelchair. I'm stuck with stairs."

sources: UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
